description_ru: Три линии защиты организма: барьеры, врождённый и приобретённый иммунитет, а также аллергии и здоровые привычки.
text:
Imagine a castle surrounded by walls, guarded by soldiers, and equipped with a network of messengers that can call for help within minutes. This is a good picture of your immune system. It is not one organ, but a team of cells, tissues and chemical signals spread throughout the entire body, and it works day and night to keep you healthy. Most of the time you do not notice it, in the same way that you do not notice a good security guard until something goes wrong.

The first line of defence is physical. Your skin is a waterproof barrier that few germs can cross, and it is also slightly acidic and covered with harmless bacteria that compete with dangerous ones. Inside your nose, sticky mucus traps dust and microbes, and tiny hairs sweep it away. Your eyes make tears that contain a substance able to break open bacteria, and the strong acid in your stomach destroys many germs that arrive with your food. When you sneeze or cough, you are using a reflex that expels unwanted visitors.

If a germ gets through these barriers, the second line of defence, called the innate immune system, reacts within minutes. It does not need to recognise the specific invader. Special white blood cells known as neutrophils and macrophages rush to the place of the problem and swallow harmful microbes. This is why a small cut becomes red, warm and swollen. Blood vessels widen to bring more cells to the area, and fluid leaks into the tissue. That unpleasant inflammation is actually a sign that your body is fighting back.

Fever is another part of the response. When your cells detect an infection, they release chemical messengers that tell the brain to raise the body's temperature, usually to about thirty-eight or thirty-nine degrees. Many bacteria and viruses multiply more slowly in the heat, while some immune cells work faster. This does not mean that every fever should be allowed to continue. A very high temperature, or one that lasts more than a few days, requires a doctor. But a mild fever is not an illness. It is a tool.

The third line of defence is the adaptive immune system, which is slower but much more precise. It relies on two main types of white blood cells, called B cells and T cells. B cells produce antibodies, tiny proteins shaped to fit a particular germ like a key in a lock. T cells have two jobs: some help to coordinate the response, and others destroy cells that have already been infected. Most importantly, after the infection is over, a few of these cells remain as memory cells. This is why you rarely catch chickenpox twice.

Sometimes, however, the immune system makes mistakes. In an allergy, it reacts strongly to something harmless, such as pollen, peanuts or cat hair, and this causes sneezing, itching or, in serious cases, a dangerous swelling. In autoimmune diseases, such as type 1 diabetes, the body attacks its own healthy tissue by mistake. In other cases, the system is weak, either because a person is born with a defect or because a disease, such as HIV, damages it. In all these cases, doctors try to adjust the response without removing protection.

How can we support our immune system? There is no magic food or supplement that will "boost" it, whatever advertisements may say. But the basics matter. Studies show that people who sleep less than six hours are more likely to catch colds, because sleep helps the body to produce protective proteins. Regular exercise, a varied diet with enough vitamins and a calm approach to stress also help. Washing your hands remains one of the simplest and most effective ways to reduce the number of germs you meet.

Age changes the picture as well. Babies are born with only a basic defence, and they borrow antibodies from their mother, first through the placenta and later through breast milk. As children grow, every cold and infection adds a new entry to their immune memory, which is one reason why young children seem to be ill so often. In old age, the system gradually becomes slower, which explains why older people are more at risk from infections and why they benefit so much from protection.

Finally, vaccines are an important partner of the immune system, because they train it in advance. But even without them, your body has an extraordinary ability to defend itself. If you stop to think about it, millions of cells are cooperating at this very moment, without any instructions from you, to keep you alive. Perhaps that is a good reason to treat your body with a little more gratitude, and to give it the rest it needs when it says that it is tired.

questions.question: What is the first line of defence?
questions.answer: Physical barriers such as skin, mucus, tears and stomach acid.

questions.question: Why does the body develop a fever?
questions.answer: Heat slows many germs and makes some immune cells work faster.

questions.question: What actually helps the immune system?
questions.answer: Sleep, exercise, a varied diet, less stress and hand washing.
